I have a background in backend development, database engineering, and AI/ML, with experience at Infosys and Stanford's Code in Place mentorship program. I'm passionate about AI, space exploration, and building impactful solutions. I'm looking to collaborate with AI/ML enthusiasts, frontend developers, UI/UX designers, and healthcare or space science experts .
summary:
SpaceHealth is a web-based health monitoring system for astronauts on a Mars mission, built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It recognises that astronaut health needs change between the long interplanetary flight and life on the Martian surface, so users first choose their mission environment and then get a dashboard and records tailored to that phase.

Astronauts can log blood pressure, heart rate, oxygen saturation, temperature, weight and notes through a manual entry form. The dashboard summarises recent readings and raises clear warnings when averages leave the normal range, so problems are noticed early. Sleep data is tracked as a seven-day average, shown green at six hours or more and flagged red below that.

An analytics view charts blood pressure over 30 days and highlights out-of-range readings. Blood and urine lab results can be uploaded, and key markers such as glucose, calcium and creatinine appear as colour-coded cards with plain-language guidance.

The frontend uses React and Vite, while the backend uses FastAPI and SQLAlchemy with a SQLite database. Together they form a lightweight system that can run on modest hardware, which suits the limited resources of a spacecraft.

All health ranges and tips are demonstration guidance, not medical advice. In a real mission, flight surgeons would set the limits.
details:
SpaceHealth: Astronaut Health Monitoring System

A detailed project essay for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026: Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions

1. Introduction and problem statement

A journey to Mars is the longest and most isolated human mission ever planned. Astronauts will spend roughly half a year in transit, live and work on the Martian surface, and be too far from Earth for real-time medical help. Radio signals between the two planets take minutes in each direction, so a crew cannot simply call a doctor and wait for an answer. Health monitoring therefore has to work close to the astronaut: simple to use, quick to show what has changed, and clear about what to do next.

SpaceHealth is a software prototype built to explore that need. It is a web application where astronauts record their own health measurements, see recent trends at a glance, receive automatic warnings when values drift outside normal ranges, and review lab results in plain language. The project responds directly to the challenge of creating health monitoring software for astronauts on space missions.

2. Design philosophy

Three ideas shaped the project.

Mission awareness. An astronaut's situation changes radically between phases. During interplanetary flight the concerns are microgravity effects, sleep, and bone and muscle loss. On the surface the concerns include radiation and the thin, cold environment. SpaceHealth therefore asks the user at the start where they are, either in space flight or at Mars, and then shows a dashboard, module list and data set for that phase.

Clarity over volume. Astronauts are busy and often tired. The dashboard reduces many readings to a few headline numbers with a clear status, and shows a red warning only when something needs attention. Lab results are shown as cards with a colour and a short explanation, not as raw tables.

Independence. Because help is delayed, the software gives practical first guidance, such as drinking enough fluids or doing resistance exercise, and tells the user when to consult the on-board health specialist or ask the ground station.

3. System overview

SpaceHealth has three layers.

  • Frontend: a single-page application written in React and built with Vite. It uses Lucide icons and hand-drawn SVG for charts, so it needs no heavy charting library.
  • Backend: a REST API written in Python with FastAPI and SQLAlchemy. It stores records, computes summaries and applies the warning rules.
  • Database: SQLite, a single-file database that needs no separate server.

The frontend talks to the backend over HTTP using JSON. The backend is organised into routers, one each for health records, lab results and sleep sensor data, plus summary endpoints defined in the main application file. Models describe the tables, and a startup step creates the tables automatically.

4. Features in detail

4.1 Mission selection

The landing page presents two cards, Space Flight (interplanetary transit) and At Mars (Martian operations). The choice is remembered for the browser session and is validated when the app loads, so a stale value cannot break the page. Every record is tagged with its mission type, and the dashboard requests only the data for the chosen mission. A single button lets the user switch missions.

4.2 Dashboard and warnings

The dashboard shows four headline cards: heart rate, oxygen level, sleep duration and blood pressure. For heart rate, oxygen saturation and blood pressure, the backend averages the readings from the last two days. If nothing was recorded in that window, it falls back to the most recent day that has data, and the card says so, so the user never mistakes old data for fresh data.

Each average is compared with a normal range. A heart rate average outside 60 to 100 beats per minute or an oxygen average below 95 percent produces a red warning such as "HR too high" or "SpO2 too low". An unusually high oxygen value is flagged as a possible sensor problem. Blood pressure is checked for both the systolic and diastolic number. Warning status is computed from the exact average, not the rounded one, so a borderline value such as 59.6 beats per minute is not hidden by rounding.

These ranges are collected in one place in the backend and can be changed by a clinician without touching the interface.

4.3 Manual health entry and records

A manual entry form lets the astronaut record blood pressure, heart rate, oxygen saturation, temperature, weight and a free-text note. Each submission is saved with a timestamp and appears immediately on the dashboard and in the Health Records list, newest first. Notes allow context that numbers cannot carry, for example "felt dizzy after exercise".

4.4 Sleep monitoring

Sleep is one of the most important and most disrupted aspects of life in space. The backend reads nightly sleep hours from a dedicated sleep sensor table and computes the average over the last seven days. At six hours or more the dashboard shows a green "Sleep is healthy" message. Below six hours it shows a red "Sleep too low" warning. The card also states how many readings the average is based on.

4.5 Analytics and reports

The analytics view contains a 30-day blood pressure chart with separate lines for systolic and diastolic pressure. Readings outside the normal range are circled in red, and hovering over a point shows the exact time and value. A short sentence above the chart summarises the number of readings, the average, and how many fall outside the range. The chart is drawn directly as SVG and adapts its vertical scale to the data.

4.6 Lab data upload and marker cards

Blood and urine results can be uploaded from spreadsheet files and are stored in a lab results table. The analytics page then shows cards for fasting glucose, calcium and creatinine, using the newest value for each. Every card is classified into one of three bands: green for normal, yellow for borderline, and red for out of range. Each shows the value, the normal range and a "Read more" section with guidance that depends on the result and its direction. For example, low calcium prompts resistance exercise to protect bone, while high creatinine prompts attention to hydration and a check of the full kidney profile. If a file uses a unit the card does not support, the card says so instead of showing a misleading status.

4.7 Planned modules

The dashboard also lists modules for mental wellness, physical activity, radiation exposure and environmental health. These currently open a "coming soon" page. They show the intended direction: a complete picture of crew health across body, mind and environment.

5. Technical implementation

5.1 Frontend

The main application component handles mission selection and the dashboard, while separate components handle manual entry, data upload and analytics. State is managed with React hooks. Data loading uses effects that cancel stale requests, so switching missions quickly cannot display the wrong data. The save function surfaces clear error messages from the server, including when the server returns something other than JSON.

5.2 Backend

FastAPI provides automatic interactive documentation, which made testing endpoints easy during development. The summary endpoints query the database with SQLAlchemy and apply the averaging and status rules in Python. Cross-origin access is restricted to local development addresses. Timestamps are stored in UTC and treated that way throughout, which avoids errors caused by time zones.

5.3 Data model

There are three tables. Health records hold the mission type, blood pressure, heart rate, oxygen saturation, temperature, weight, notes and a timestamp. Lab results hold the test name, value, unit, sample type and measurement date. Sleep sensor readings hold a date and the hours slept. A seed script generates thirty days of realistic sample data, including occasional abnormal readings, so charts and warnings can be demonstrated without waiting for real data.

6. Development process and lessons

The project grew in stages: first the mission-aware interface and manual entry, then the two-day averages and warnings, then sleep, then analytics and lab cards. Several practical lessons came out of it.

  • A React hook called outside a component crashed the whole page, which showed how small mistakes can stop an entire interface.
  • A mismatch between a guessed column name and the real database model made a feature silently show nothing. Checking the actual model fixed it.
  • Charts with almost no data look broken, so a seed script for realistic history was essential for testing and demonstration.
  • Computing warnings from rounded numbers can hide problems, so thresholds should always be applied to exact values.

7. Limitations

SpaceHealth is a prototype, and being honest about its limits matters in a health context.

  • It currently serves a single user and has no login or role separation, which a real mission would need.
  • Data is entered by hand or uploaded. It does not yet connect to wearable devices or on-board sensors.
  • The normal ranges and health tips are demonstration guidance and are not medical advice. In a real mission, flight surgeons would define the limits for each astronaut.
  • Sleep data is not yet separated by mission phase.
  • The SQLite database suits a prototype, but a multi-crew deployment would need a more robust database and backups.
  • Several dashboard modules are placeholders.

8. Future work

  • Live sensor integration for heart rate, oxygen saturation and sleep, so data arrives automatically.
  • Per-astronaut profiles with personalised baselines, since a normal value for one person may be unusual for another.
  • Trend-based alerts that warn when a value is changing quickly, not only when it crosses a fixed line.
  • Radiation exposure tracking with cumulative dose limits, and environmental monitoring on the surface.
  • Mental wellness check-ins for mood, stress and isolation.
  • Offline-first operation and delayed synchronisation with the ground station, to cope with communication gaps.
  • Authentication, encryption and audit logs to protect sensitive medical data.
  • A deployed hosted version with a live demo, a proper production database and automated tests.

9. Ethical and safety considerations

Medical data is among the most sensitive information a person has. A real system would need strong privacy protections and clear rules on who can see an astronaut's records. Automated warnings can also be wrong, so SpaceHealth presents them as prompts to check and consult, never as diagnoses. Keeping a human medical expert in the loop is a deliberate design principle.

10. Conclusion

SpaceHealth shows how a lightweight, mission-aware tool can help astronauts understand their own health when expert help is far away. It combines easy data entry, clear warnings, sleep tracking, trend charts and readable lab results in one interface, built from open-source tools that run on modest hardware. It is a prototype with real limits, but it demonstrates a workable foundation for monitoring astronaut wellness during the journey to Mars and on its surface, and it points to a clear path for turning the idea into a dependable system.
